final_proof:
Let $f(t) = u(t) + i v(t)$, where $u, v: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ are the real and imaginary parts of $f$. Since $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, it follows that $u$ and $v$ are continuous real-valued functions on $[a, b]$.

By definition, the integral of a complex-valued function of a real variable over an interval $[x, y]$ is defined as:
$$\int_x^y f(t) dt = \int_x^y u(t) dt + i \int_x^y v(t) dt$$

Applying this definition to the intervals $[a, c]$ and $[c, b]$, we have:
$$\int_a^c f(t) dt = \int_a^c u(t) dt + i \int_a^c v(t) dt$$
and
$$\int_c^b f(t) dt = \int_c^b u(t) dt + i \int_c^b v(t) dt$$

Adding these two equations together yields:
$$\int_a^c f(t) dt + \int_c^b f(t) dt = \left( \int_a^c u(t) dt + i \int_a^c v(t) dt \right) + \left( \int_c^b u(t) dt + i \int_c^b v(t) dt \right)$$

Regrouping the real and imaginary components gives:
$$\int_a^c f(t) dt + \int_c^b f(t) dt = \left( \int_a^c u(t) dt + \int_c^b u(t) dt \right) + i \left( \int_a^c v(t) dt + \int_c^b v(t) dt \right)$$

Since $u$ and $v$ are continuous real functions on $[a, b]$ and $c \in [a, b]$, we can apply the additivity property of the definite integral for real-valued functions on adjacent intervals:
$$\int_a^c u(t) dt + \int_c^b u(t) dt = \int_a^b u(t) dt$$
and
$$\int_a^c v(t) dt + \int_c^b v(t) dt = \int_a^b v(t) dt$$

Substituting these results back into our expression, we obtain:
$$\int_a^c f(t) dt + \int_c^b f(t) dt = \int_a^b u(t) dt + i \int_a^b v(t) dt$$

Finally, by the definition of the complex integral, the right-hand side is exactly equal to $\int_a^b f(t) dt$. Therefore, we conclude that:
$$\int_a^c f(t) dt + \int_c^b f(t) dt = \int_a^b f(t) dt$$
which completes the proof.
